456.title: Two are better than one (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12)
456.hook: if one falls, the other lifts; a threefold cord is not quickly broken
456.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 is a common reading at Christian weddings, where the threefold cord is often explained as husband, wife and God; some couples braid three cords during the ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher's list of seasons, and your line was a time for everything. What time is it for you this week? Day four hundred fifty-six.

Right before today's passage, the Preacher describes a man who has no one. No son, no brother. And there's no end to his work, the text says, and his eyes are never satisfied with his money. He never stops to ask who all this is for. It's a sharp little portrait, and it could be someone you know: the one who answers emails at midnight, eats at the desk, and hasn't called a friend in a year. The Preacher has been looking hard at everything under the sun and finding most of it breath. But then, in the middle of all that hevel, he finds something that holds. Today, the thing that holds.
screen: `A MAN WITH NO ONE.` → `NO END TO HIS WORK.` → `WHO IS THIS FOR?` → `SOMETHING THAT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour." Then the Preacher gives three pictures, all very physical. First, the fall: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." Think of a road at night, a ditch, a twisted ankle. Second, the cold: two people lying together keep each other warm, but how can one be warm alone? In the desert, nights get cold, and travelers shared blankets and body heat. Third, the attack: someone might overpower a person alone, but two can stand against him. Fall, cold, danger. In each one, a second person is the difference. Then, almost as a proverb tacked on the end, the line your carry comes from: "and a threefold cord is not quickly broken." Twist two strands together and they're stronger. Twist in a third and the rope holds far more. It's how rope is actually made. Notice the Preacher counted two, and then the proverb says three. Readers have wondered about that. Many Christians, especially at weddings, hear the third strand as God, woven in with the couple. Others hear it simply as a proverb about community: two is good, more is better. The text itself doesn't say who the third strand is. But it's a striking moment. The Preacher who called everything breath doesn't call friendship breath. In a book that doubts almost everything, he's sure of this.
screen: `A MAN ALONE, WORKING FOR NO ONE.` · `IF ONE FALLS, THE OTHER LIFTS.` · `TWO KEEP WARM; TWO STAND FIRM.` · `A THREEFOLD CORD.` · then, large: `TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a friend, first in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who once lifted you when you fell: a hard week, a bad diagnosis, a breakup, a day you couldn't get off the couch. See their face. Remember one specific thing they did, the call, the meal, the ride, the hour they just sat there. Let yourself feel how cold that time would have been alone. Then think of the words you'd use to thank them, simple and plain. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Two are better than one. The Preacher's three pictures: one to lift, one to warm, one to stand beside you, and a cord of three strands that does not quickly break.
screen: `TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a threefold cord. Today, send the thank-you. Tell one friend the specific time they lifted you, and that you haven't forgotten. Day four hundred fifty-six.

457.title: Remember now your creator (Ecclesiastes 12:1–8)
457.hook: before the silver cord is loosed
457.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 12 is read at some Christian funerals, especially for older people, and its opening verse is often taught to young people in churches and youth groups as a call not to put faith off until later.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher found something that holds, and your line was a threefold cord. Did you thank the friend who lifted you? Day four hundred fifty-seven.

Picture a big old house at the end of a day. The guards at the door have started to tremble. The strong men are stooped. The women who grind the grain have stopped, because there are too few of them left. The ones who look out of the windows find everything dim. The doors to the street are shut, and the sound of the mill is low. Someone wakes at the first chirp of a bird. The almond tree is in bloom, all white. It sounds like a ghost story. It's actually a riddle, and the Preacher expects you to solve it. He's describing a body growing old. Today, the last poem in his book.
screen: `A HOUSE AT THE END OF THE DAY.` → `THE GRINDERS CEASE.` → `IT'S A RIDDLE.` → `A BODY GROWING OLD.`

segments.voice: The poem opens, in the King James Bible: "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them." Then comes the riddle of the house. Many readers, ancient and modern, decode it like this. The keepers of the house who tremble are the hands and arms. The strong men bowing are the legs and back. The grinders that cease because they are few are the teeth. Those who look out of the windows are the eyes. Waking at the sound of a bird is light sleep in old age. And the almond tree in white blossom is white hair. Not every reader takes each image the same way, and some hear a whole town falling into ruin as well as a body. But the point lands either way. Then the images turn to endings: "Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken." A lamp hanging on a silver chain, the chain snaps, the golden bowl of oil shatters, the light goes out. A pitcher breaks at the well. And then: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." Now go back to the first word, remember. In Hebrew it's not only recalling a fact. It means to keep someone in mind and act on it, the way God remembers Noah in the flood and sends the wind. So remember your Creator isn't nostalgia. It's: live toward God now, while your hands are steady and your eyes are clear. The Preacher isn't trying to frighten the young. He's urging them not to wait.
screen: `REMEMBER, IN THE DAYS OF YOUTH.` · `A RIDDLE: HANDS, TEETH, EYES, HAIR.` · `THE SILVER CORD, THE GOLDEN BOWL.` · `REMEMBER MEANS ACT ON IT.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT SHALL RETURN UNTO GOD WHO GAVE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you can still do, today. Settle, and breathe. Feel your hands. Open and close them slowly. Notice your eyes taking in light, your ears catching small sounds. Whatever your age, there are things your body can do right now that it may not always do. Then bring to mind one thing you've been putting off for later: a visit, a call, a walk, a promise, a prayer. Let the Preacher's question sit with you: why not now? If you pray, you can offer today's strength back to the One who gave it. The bell holds the time.
Remember now your creator. The Preacher's last poem: keep God in mind and act on it while you're young, before the silver cord is loosed.
Your line: remember, while you're young. Whatever your age, you're younger today than you'll ever be again. Do the one thing you've been saving for later, while you can. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

458.title: Love as strong as death (Song of Songs 8:6–7)
458.hook: many waters cannot quench love; a book of love poetry in the Bible
458.howItsDone: Song of Songs 8:6–7 is a frequent reading at Christian weddings; the book has a long history of devotional reading as a picture of God's love, and in Jewish practice it is read at Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher's last poem, remember now your Creator, and your line was remember, while you're young. Did you do the thing you'd been saving for later? Day four hundred fifty-eight.

Some people open the Bible expecting rules and are startled to find this. A woman searching the city streets at night for the one she loves. A man comparing her hair to a flock of goats coming down a mountainside, which was a compliment. Gardens, spices, vineyards, doves, a knock at the door. Two voices, longing for each other, out loud. It's a whole book of love poetry, eight chapters long, sitting right after Ecclesiastes. And near its end, the woman says something so strong that people still put it on wedding invitations and gravestones. Today, the line that ties love and death together.
screen: `SEARCHING THE CITY AT NIGHT.` → `HAIR LIKE A FLOCK OF GOATS.` → `A WHOLE BOOK OF LOVE POETRY.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death." A seal in the ancient world was a stamp carved in stone, worn on a cord around the neck or on a ring. It was your signature, your identity. To say set me as a seal on your heart is to say: carry me, let me be the mark you press into everything. And then, love is as strong as death. Not stronger. As strong. Death is the one thing nothing escapes, and love, she says, holds on just as hard. Then the next verse: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." In the Bible, the great waters are chaos, the flood, the sea that swallows. Love isn't put out by them. And one more line: if a man offered everything he owned for love, he'd be laughed at. Love can't be bought. Now, a surprise: God is barely named in this book, if at all. Some read one word in verse six, describing love's flame, as containing a short form of God's name; many others read it simply as a mighty flame. So why is it in the Bible? Readers have answered in more than one way. Jewish tradition has long read it as the love between God and Israel; a famous rabbi called it the holy of holies among the writings. Many Christians, from the early church on, have read it as the love between Christ and the church, or God and the soul. And many readers today also honor it as what it plainly is: human love, desire and faithfulness, celebrated as good.
screen: `SET ME AS A SEAL UPON THINE HEART.` · `AS STRONG AS DEATH, NOT STRONGER.` · `MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE.` · `GOD, ISRAEL, CHRIST, OR TWO PEOPLE?` · then, large: `LOVE IS STRONG AS DEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one love that has lasted. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you love: a partner, a parent, a child, a friend of many years. Think of the floods it has come through: a move, an argument, an illness, a long silence, a loss. Notice that it's still here. Picture them carrying you like a seal on the heart, and you carrying them. Let yourself feel how much you love them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them, by name. The bell holds the time.
Love as strong as death. From the Song of Songs: love that holds on as hard as death does, and that no flood can put out.
screen: `LOVE AS STRONG AS DEATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: many waters cannot quench love. Today, tell someone you love them, in plain words, out loud or written down. Don't wait for the occasion. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

459.title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
459.hook: in a book of ruins: his mercies are new every morning
459.howItsDone: Many Christians sing the hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness, drawn from Lamentations 3:22–23, and some read the verses at the start of the day; in Jewish practice the whole book of Lamentations is chanted on Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a book of love poetry, and your line was many waters cannot quench love. Who did you tell? Day four hundred fifty-nine.

Jerusalem has fallen. The Babylonian army has broken through the walls, burned the Temple, and marched much of the city's population away. The streets that were full are empty. Children faint from hunger at the corners. The roads to the city mourn, the text says, because no one comes to the feasts anymore. Someone sat in that ruin and wrote five poems about it. They are the book of Lamentations, and they are some of the rawest grief anywhere in the Bible. No tidy answers. Long stretches of pain. And then, right in the middle of the middle poem, a line so hopeful that many churches sing it, often with no idea where it came from. Today, that line.
screen: `JERUSALEM HAS FALLEN.` → `FIVE POEMS OF GRIEF.` → `A LINE OF HOPE IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Before it, the poet is at the bottom. He says he's been walled in, that his prayers are shut out, that he's forgotten what happiness is. Then he says he's going to call something to mind, and hope rises from it. In the King James Bible: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Look closely at what he doesn't say. He doesn't say the city is rebuilt. It isn't. He doesn't say the grief is over. It goes on for two more chapters. He says one thing has not run out: God's mercies, in Hebrew chasadim, steadfast loving-kindness. They are new every morning. Not stored up from yesterday, not a fixed supply that gets used up. Delivered fresh, like the manna in the desert that had to be gathered each day. There's a detail in the shape of the book. Four of the five poems are acrostics, each verse or stanza starting with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The third poem, where this line sits, is the most intense: three verses for every letter, sixty-six in all. Grief, put in order, letter by letter, from A to Z, as if to say: we will grieve this completely. And right at the center of it, this. The book's author isn't named in the text; an old tradition credits the prophet Jeremiah. Jewish communities read Lamentations each year on Tisha B'Av, mourning the Temple's fall. And in 1923 a Methodist writer named Thomas Chisholm drew on this line for a hymn, Great Is Thy Faithfulness, that many churches still sing.
screen: `THE POET AT THE BOTTOM.` · `THE CITY ISN'T REBUILT.` · `MERCIES NEW EVERY MORNING.` · `GRIEF IN ORDER, LETTER BY LETTER.` · then, large: `GREAT IS THY FAITHFULNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let tomorrow begin fresh. Settle, and breathe. Think of the ruin in your own week: a mistake you made, a hurt you carried, a thing that didn't get fixed. Don't pretend it isn't there. The poet didn't. Then picture tomorrow morning: light coming in, the first breath of the day. Imagine waking without dragging today's weight into it, not because it's solved, but because the morning is new. If you pray, you can say the line itself: great is thy faithfulness. The bell holds the time.
New every morning. From the middle of Lamentations: in a ruined city, God's mercies don't run out; they come fresh each day.
Your line: new every morning. Tonight, before you sleep, set down one thing from today on purpose. Tomorrow, when you wake, say the line once before you check your phone. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

460.title: The books between (Wisdom 3:1–3)
460.hook: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Wisdom, Sirach and others; Protestants often call them Apocrypha
460.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians read the deuterocanonical books in worship, and Wisdom 3:1–9 is a common reading at Catholic funerals; Anglican and Episcopal churches read from the Apocrypha in their lectionaries, while many other Protestant churches read them privately, if at all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a line of hope in a book of ruins, and your line was new every morning. Did you set something down last night? Day four hundred sixty.

Put three Bibles side by side on a table: one from a Catholic parish, one from a Greek Orthodox church, one from a Baptist church down the street. Open each to the table of contents. They all begin with Genesis. They all end with Revelation. But count the books, and the counts don't match. The Protestant Bible has sixty-six. The Catholic Bible has seventy-three. Orthodox Bibles have a few more again. Same faith in Christ, same Gospels, different shelves. If you've ever wondered why, today is the day. It's about a handful of books from the centuries just before Jesus, and what each church calls them.
screen: `THREE BIBLES ON A TABLE.` → `SIXTY-SIX, SEVENTY-THREE, AND MORE.` → `WHY DON'T THE COUNTS MATCH?`

segments.voice: The extra books include Tobit, Judith, the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, and First and Second Maccabees, plus extra passages in Esther and Daniel. Most were written, or survive, in Greek, and they were part of the Greek Old Testament that many early Christians read. Catholics call them deuterocanonical: deutero means second, canon means the measuring rule, the list. Second-listed, not second-rate: it means their place on the list was settled later, after some debate. The Council of Trent confirmed them for Catholics in 1546. Orthodox churches also read them, and include a few others. In the Reformation, Martin Luther gathered these books into their own section between the testaments, saying they weren't equal to scripture but were useful and good to read. Many Protestants call them the Apocrypha, from a Greek word for hidden. The 1611 King James Bible itself printed them, between the testaments, and Anglicans still read from them in worship. So: who says what. Catholics and Orthodox Christians hold them as scripture. Many Protestants honor them as edifying history and wisdom but not as scripture. Now, a taste of one. The Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek, speaks about good people who die young or unjustly. In the King James Apocrypha: "But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and there shall no torment touch them." To the foolish, the passage goes on, they seemed to die, but they are in peace. It's read at funerals across traditions. Whatever shelf you keep it on, it's a line people have held at gravesides for a very long time.
screen: `TOBIT, JUDITH, WISDOM, SIRACH.` · `DEUTERO: SECOND-LISTED, NOT SECOND-RATE.` · `TRENT, LUTHER, AND THE KING JAMES.` · `WHO HOLDS THEM AS SCRIPTURE.` · then, large: `THE SOULS OF THE RIGHTEOUS ARE IN THE HAND OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line slowly, and hold someone with it. Settle, and breathe. Let the line come back: the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God. Read it again in your mind, slowly, word by word. Then bring to mind someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to. Picture them held, not lost. If you pray, you can entrust them to God with the line itself. If you don't, just sit with them for a moment, in that picture of an open hand. The bell holds the time.
Deuterocanon. The second-listed books, like Wisdom and Sirach: scripture for Catholics and the Orthodox, the Apocrypha for many Protestants.
Your line: in the hand of god. Today, when you think of someone you've lost, or someone you're worried about, picture them there: in a hand, held. Day four hundred sixty.

461.title: Block close: the prayer book
461.hook: psalms for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good
461.howItsDone: Christians pray the Psalms daily in many forms: monastic communities and the Liturgy of the Hours cycle through them, Orthodox services read the whole Psalter each week, Anglicans pray them through each month, and many Protestants read one a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the books between, the deuterocanon, and your line was in the hand of god. Who did you picture held there? Day four hundred sixty-one.

Fifty days ago we opened this part of the Bible with a tree planted by the water. Since then: a psalm for the night sky and a psalm for the dark night. A cry of my God, my God, why. A deer panting for water. A clean heart, asked for after a terrible failure. Help from the hills. Out of the depths. By the rivers of Babylon. Let everything that has breath. Then Job, a good man who lost everything, and the friends who were wise for seven days and then started talking. Proverbs and its ant. The Preacher and his breath. Love as strong as death. A morning mercy in a ruined city. Today we close the block, and look at what all of it was.
screen: `FIFTY DAYS SINCE THE TREE.` → `PSALMS, JOB, PROVERBS.` → `THE PREACHER AND THE SONG.` → `WHAT WAS ALL OF IT?`

segments.voice: Start with the Psalms. For many centuries they have been the prayer book of Jews and of Christians: monks chant all hundred and fifty in a cycle, churches sing them on Sunday, people whisper them in hospital beds. And the surprise, every time, is how much of it isn't polite. There is joy, in the King James words: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." There is trust: the Lord is my shepherd. But there is also rage, and confusion, and how long, O Lord, and one psalm, the eighty-eighth, that ends in darkness with no answer at all. A large share of the psalms are laments. The Bible's prayer book teaches you to bring the real feeling, not the tidy one. The early church writer Athanasius said that most of scripture speaks to us, but the Psalms speak for us: you find your own words already there. Then the wisdom books, and they keep the same honesty. Job won't accept a cheap answer for suffering, and God, in the end, says Job spoke rightly and his explainers did not. Proverbs says ordinary life, the tongue, the work, the ant, is where wisdom happens. The Preacher says life is breath, and therefore to eat your bread with joy. The Song says love is as strong as death. Lamentations says the mercies are new every morning, even in the ruins. Put all of that together and you get one idea: everything a human being feels can be brought before God. Christians of every church have prayed this way, and so has Jesus, who prayed a psalm on the cross. The prayer book was never meant to make you sound holy. It was meant to make you honest.
screen: `THE PRAYER BOOK OF TWO FAITHS.` · `NOT POLITE: RAGE, GRIEF, PRAISE.` · `THE PSALMS SPEAK FOR US.` · `WISDOM KEEPS THE SAME HONESTY.` · then, large: `PRAY WHAT YOU FEEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one psalm to keep all year. Settle, and breathe. Let some of them pass by in your mind: the tree by the water, the Lord is my shepherd, as the deer, be still, I lift up my eyes, out of the depths, you knit me together. Notice which one your heart leans toward. Not the one you think you should choose. The one that sounds like you. When it comes, keep it. That's your psalm for the year, for good days and bad. If you pray, you can pray its first line now. The bell holds the time.
Block close. Fifty days of psalms and wisdom: a prayer book for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short, and good.

Your line: pray what you feel. Today, write your psalm's number somewhere you'll see it, and the next time a strong feeling comes, good or hard, bring it to God or to the page exactly as it is. Day four hundred sixty-one.

original.note: Hebrew name of the book of Psalms: praises, though many of them are laments.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Psalms are gentle, holy-sounding prayers.

462.title: What a prophet is
462.hook: one who speaks for God, usually uncomfortably, to their own people
462.howItsDone: Christians read the prophets throughout the church year, especially in Advent and Lent, and many churches see the prophets' call for justice as part of their own work with the poor; Jewish communities read a passage from the Prophets, the haftarah, every Sabbath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block close on the prayer book, and your line was pray what you feel. Which psalm did you choose to keep? Day four hundred sixty-two.

A king has done something terrible. He took another man's wife, and when she became pregnant, he arranged for her husband to die in battle. It's covered up. Nobody at court will say a word. Then a man named Nathan asks for an audience and tells the king a story: a rich man with huge flocks steals a poor man's only lamb, a lamb the poor man's children loved, to serve to a guest. The king is furious. That man deserves to die, he says. And Nathan looks at King David and says four words, in the King James Bible: "Thou art the man." Today, a new block of the path: the prophets. And the first question: what is a prophet?
screen: `A KING'S COVER-UP.` → `A STORY ABOUT A STOLEN LAMB.` → `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Most people today think a prophet is someone who predicts the future. In the Bible, that's a small part of it. The Greek word prophetes means one who speaks for, or speaks forth: a spokesperson. The Hebrew is navi, and scholars think it means one who is called, or one who calls out. Either way, the job is less fortune-telling than forth-telling: saying what God sees, now, out loud. Now notice who they spoke to. The prophets mostly spoke to their own people. Not to enemies. To their own kings, their own priests, their own neighbors, about their own injustice: the poor cheated in the market, widows ignored, worship that was all show. It was rarely welcome. Jeremiah was beaten and thrown in a pit. Amos was told to go home. Many weren't professionals at all. Amos said he was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but a herdsman and a tender of fig trees. Ordinary people, called to say an uncomfortable thing. And they weren't only stern. The same voices that warned also comforted: Isaiah, whom we meet tomorrow, will speak of swords beaten into plowshares, and of a God who will not forget his people even if a mother could forget her child. In Christian Bibles, the prophets come at the end of the Old Testament: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel and Daniel, called the major prophets because their books are long, then twelve shorter ones. Jewish Bibles arrange them differently, and count books like Joshua and Kings among the prophets too. Jesus himself was called a prophet by the crowds, and said, "A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house." Christians honor him as more than a prophet, but they also see him standing in this line.
screen: `NOT FORETELLING: FORTH-TELLING.` · `TO THEIR OWN PEOPLE.` · `A HERDSMAN, NOT A PROFESSIONAL.` · `MAJOR MEANS LONG, NOT IMPORTANT.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one uncomfortable truth. Settle, and breathe. Think of something someone has told you recently that stung: a criticism from a friend, a complaint from your partner, a hard word from a boss, a line in the news that pointed straight at people like you. Notice your first reaction, the defense forming. Set it aside for a moment. Ask honestly: is there any truth in it? Not all of it. Just any. Hold that piece without arguing. If you pray, you can ask for ears to hear it. The bell holds the time.
Prophet. Navi in Hebrew, prophetes in Greek: one called to speak for God, usually uncomfortably, and usually to their own people.
Your line: truth to power. Today, when someone tells you something you don't want to hear, listen all the way to the end before you answer. Day four hundred sixty-two.

tell the king a story, then say thou art the man.

fork.reveal: Nathan tells a story about a stolen lamb, lets the king judge it, and then says "thou art the man." truth to power, to his own king.

original.note: Hebrew: a prophet. scholars think it means one who is called, or one who calls out.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophet is someone who predicts the future.
what it means: someone called to speak for God, usually an uncomfortable word, usually to their own people.

what a scholar hears: navi likely from a root meaning to call. the Greek prophetes is a spokesperson. and in the Hebrew Bible the Prophets include Joshua through Kings, while Daniel sits among the Writings.
